Curious whether the prevailing sentiment for today’s comments will be ALL THOSE AGAINST or ARENT YOU SPECIAL—or maybe The Sound and The Fury.

For me it was more of A Tale of Two Puzzles, or maybe three or four or more. There was the inexplicable gimme of GENERAL ELECTION this time of year, and other inexplicable gimmes for a Saturday like ATOLLS and DALAI and ALIST and COOTIES and lots more. There were the other spanners which were decent entries but oddly very blandly clued. There were a few misdirects for me like MOVE before MORE, KICK before WASH, BAND before ROAD for Journey, ICECAPADE and ICEPARADE before ICEPALACE. 

There were a few entries I smiled at like SCHMOOZED  POM and MASSEMAIL (I had MAILBLAST first, but either way it certainly brings back fond or not so fond memories of your own or someone else’s faux pas.) And there were a few clues that I thought were more stretchy for their own good like LONGE (I don’t mind a good phonetic clue like that, but seems like a long way around for such a long title) and CONGA. But now I’m going to take CONGA back because I just got it and now it’s my favorite clue. I was imagining some Carnival cruise party with CONGA lines but then the Carnival in Rio just popped into my mind. Sam why didn’t you help us out with that one?!?

So, all in all a decent Saturday, certainly for me not as interesting as yesterday, I’m going to call it a pleasant diversion but a little all over the place.
I am recovering from a minor surgery, which already has relieved my month-long pain. And now I've just finished a wonderful Saturday puzzle. So I'm feeling good!

I was working at Wells Fargo during the infamous “Happy Birthday, Holly” mass email incident in which a well-meaning private birthday wish ended up being distributed to nearly the entire corporation. It was quite something to watch hundreds upon hundreds of reply-all emails flood everyone’s inbox with indignant demands to be removed from the distribution list. Which of course led to endless rounds of people using a reply-all email to admonish others to stop using reply-all. Frustrating. It spiraled out of control for several hours before someone found a way to shut the whole thing down. The experience was eventually turned into a media story and a t-shirt – so ultimately an amusing rather than regretful mass email memory.  What a perfect Saturday puzzle you’ve gifted us today, Mr. Juhnke, with just the right amount of bite and mischief. It pushed my current streak to 1,750 so I’m pretty chuffed about that.

On a trip to Florence in 1888 Victoria was struck in particular by a russet colored foxy-faced Volpino Italiano, a breed of spitz thought to be from Pomerania, that area of northern Poland (with its principal town Gdansk on the Baltic) and parts of Eastern Germany. She brought the dog back to England, a 12 lb. male, very playful, glowing red sable fur, naming him Marco after the Italian explorer. He was the first of many Pomeranians she owned (at one time she had over 30 of them); the last, Turi, was called in to keep her company on her death bed. Indeed, as Mr. Juhnke confirms, Victoria started a trend in England and the red sable pom was an extremely popular pet in the late 19th century. 

Andrzej, I bet you'll have something to say about this -- or I hope you will, anyway!

Another great day for constructor notes.  

Fortunately, I haven't been harmed by a "reply all", at least not yet.

But about 20 years ago I was working for a smallish startup, and the CEO sent out an email to everyone.  He was apparently having an affair with his secretary, because she made a "reply all" blunder that exposed it.   

The office was a weird combination of cringe and hilarity.  I did feel sorry for his poor secretary.  She was young and it probably still stings for her.

A perfect Saturday puzzle for a night when I had lots of time and could wait for the fills to emerge from the shadows. I wracked my brain trying to figure out what that noise was at the end of the Faulkner novel, left it for another part of the puzzle a dozen times, came back, and finally, Oh, right. Sneaky! I couldn't remember what Bubkes meant, and kept coming up with NADA, until the Lama jogged my brain. 

About those COOTIES, I recognized them right away. I brought a batch of them home when I was in 4th grade and my mother nearly fainted. She didn't know what to do, but a neighbor did and said,"Oil of sassafras 'll get em." The rude boy next door sat in a tree, watching my humiliation through the window as she combed the smelly stuff through my hair.  Thank God we moved before long.

While I was still in law school, I worked at the Warsaw office of a major, international law firm with headquarters in the US, and offices all over the world. My computer had this super unintuitive e-mail program with countless options as to who to forward messages to. Once, inevitably, while sending out some memo intended for the Warsaw office, I addressed it to every company employee all over the world... On a positive note, some of the replies I got where humorous and supportive 😃

I had no idea TEAL was a bird. I only knew the word as denoting a color. Apparently the green-winged teal is called "cyraneczka karolińska" (cyraneczka of Carolina) in Polish, a name I'm not familiar with, either. TEAL the color has been special to me for decades. When I was a pre-teen in 1990, my mom went to Stockholm on a scholarship and she brought me back some items unavailable or at least very hard to get in Poland at the time - second-hand designer jeans, a leather jacket, and a set of 30 color markers, including teal, which I've never seen before. I loved to draw with it. I was very sad when it finally ran out some time later. Growing out of that kiIIer jacket was a bummer, too.

How can Fri and Sat be so different?   I don't ever use the Internet as an aid on crosswords.   Just like the days of old it is only me, the puzzle, and a dictionary.   That said, this Friday's puzzle I found extremely hard.... It took me over 90 minutes to solve.   Compare that to today's Saturday puzzle, which to me 30 minutes to solve.    How can it be that the Saturday is that much easier than the day before. 

Or, put another way:  I found Friday's puzzle to be extremely hard (would've been much easier if I had used the Internet, as it had clues that Google wouldn't silver in a heartbeat with queries like "what did esau get from Jacob?"), while today's was relatively easy for a Saturday.     Are they making crosswords now where they expect people to look up trivia questions with Google?.... I can't figure any other way that the editors found yesterday's Friday puzzle to be easier than today's Saturday puzzle.

Fritz got on my good side in his debut Times puzzle (today is his third) with a priceless clue – [When squirrels thermoregulate by splooting].

He certainly remains there after today’s puzzle, starting with that gorgeous grid design that made me feel peaceful even before filling in the first square.

Then the drama.  Three quarters of my first pass stubbornly yielded very little, making me wonder if this was going to beat me.  But I refused to buckle, went on faith that things would break. They did in the remaining quarter, and answers leached out from there.  Overcoming adversity brings such reward.  

I remember thinking, after filling in the last square, “That was one of my best solving experiences ever!”

Icing on the cake was the serendipitous confluence of nine double-L’s.  It turns out that after A and E, the letter L today is the most populous one in the box.  Huh!

Oh yes, I loved this one, Fritz.  Please, sir, let there be more.  You do Crosslandia proud.  Thank you!

A reply all story: In my time at college, there was one of those innocuous emails that goes out to the whole school (faculty, staff, students) announcing that so and so has been hired as the new assistant dean of such and such. It didn’t mean anything to the students but clearly it came as a surprise to someone on staff who accidentally replied all “Did not see that coming!” 

This became sort of a meme for our class, and someone made stickers that said “did not see that coming” and you’d see them on laptops around campus. We were the class of 2020 so there were always a lot of vision puns being made, but this really took the cake when the way that our time at college ended was truly something nobody saw coming.

Speaking of sailing, the most surprising answer to me was using TAR to waterproof your sails.  Wouldn't it also take the wind out of your sails?  And wouldn't it be extremely ugly?  

I hate seeing that smug, snarky, completely unnecessary phrase AREN'T YOU SPECIAL in puzzles.  ALL THOSE AGAINST please raise your hands.

Re MASS EMAIL: Anyone who hits the "Reply all" button is being clueless and UNCOUTH.  Once, I think I got 40 responses to a question about what day and time worked for our high school class's alumnae Zoom meeting.  I didn't do the inviting and I didn't need to know who had a violin lesson that day and who was going to be in Cancun that week and who had a large family dinner, but could do 4:30 EST but not 5:30 EST, etc., etc, etc.  As the emails piled up, I wanted to scream out to all the people who really thought everyone cared about all the exquisite details of their social lives: AREN'T YOU SPECIAL?

But because I'm not a snarky sort of person, I didn't.

My "Reply All" story is from my first big office job (with two monitors and everything!), where I had a stinky coworker who apparently didn't believe in deodorant. I emailed a colleague joking about it. That was not a reply all, that was just a regular email.

But later that day, I was on an email thread about a problem on the website my team would need to fix, so I replied all with an attached screenshot of how it looked on my computer. But my screenshot was double-wide. It had my secondary monitor with my sent email about the office stinker. I noticed at the last possible millisecond before releasing the mouse button to click send and avoided certain disaster.

Pro tip: Always clear the "To" field empty until you're done writing and editing.

I was released from the hospital yesterday & slept much of the afternoon. I had no idea it was nearly impossible to get a good night's rest in a hospital room -- and I even had a single -- no roomie to faht and snore and otherwise keep me awake. Can you tell this is the first time I've ever spent a night in a hospital? A few nights, as it turns out.

For one day there was someone in the next room screaming for pain meds all the time, including through the night. And the nurses repeatedly explaining to her that they could give them only once every 4 hours. I empathize with the patient, but I did ask if there was any way I could be moved, so they moved me to another ward for my last night there. Sleep, at last!

My pup did well with the person who took her in for a few days. That's a relief. 

And I think the procedures have helped. My friends tell me I look better than I have in ages. They ignored all the bruises on my arms from the frequent bloodlettings. I'm not sure why they need to stab me multiple times per day when there's an IV installed. All they ever did with that, since it was unused after the first morning, was flush it and make sure it was open.

Anyway, I hope this fixes what ailed me. My heart is beating normally and my blood pressure (which I take twice per day) is better than it's been in years, which is interesting since I didn't go in to have my blood pressure fixed. 

So, I survived, things are going well and I might be here more now! Streak maintained!

Someone asked us last night if we voted in the recent primary. I was surprised at the sharp tone of my answer that came out: Of course we voted, said I! I know a lot of people don't, especially in a primary, but in Minnesota we have excellent voter turnout always and it just sort of surprised me to be questioned...  And then it truly surprised me that I was so surprised. Har!!

That said, the very same yesterday, we found out about another friend who doesn't ever vote. And that was even more shocking. And sad. And borderline infuriating....  

Anyhow, it was a fun puzzle! And I actually laughed out loud at some of the snarky, but not actually unkind, comments out here today.  I honestly wish I had even half the confidence of the folks who assert with absolute certainty that clue or answer is undeniably wrong.... when entering three lil words into their search engine of choice would show them that they in fact are wrong, not the puzzle, and they'd have had the chance to learn something. I'm with Lynn in thinking that primaries are driving our increasingly polarized country.  

They've only been around for sixty years or so.  I recall reading 40s and 50s elections, and very few states actually had a formal vote to choose a candidate.  Those few cases (New Hampshire was an early one) were used by the party bigwigs to ascertain "electability".  But the actual candidate was chosen in the proverbial "smoke-filled room".

Since then primaries have spread to nearly every state, and there's much consternation about which states get to go first (New Hampshire claims it was a pioneer, so deserves to always go first.  Iowa caucuses were once almost completely ignored, but not since the late 70s).

So primaries seem like a good idea, and they may have been at the start.

But now, as Lynn says, a "minor" election like a primary brings out only those with fervent views, and those tend to be at the extremes.  

Consider the erstwhile "moderate" party member.  Those who are willing to compromise and make deals with the other party are now threatened to be "primaried" by others in their party.  And it's a real threat.  Big time establishment politicians have been beaten in their own party.  A recent example is John Cornyn, a long time Senator from Texas was beaten by Ken Paxton.

I think every good idea eventually gets gamed to the point it's deleterious.
